1:
The birds at the altars are the difficulty of the entry, and two of them handle it in opposite ways. Adam Clarke thinks it very unlikely that sparrows and swallows should be permitted to build and hatch about altars kept in the greatest purity and served by perpetual fires, and offers three escapes: read the clause as a parenthesis, or transpose it to the end, or take the whole as a comparison, that as the sparrow finds a house and the swallow a nest for her young, so the psalmist seeks the altars. Charles Ellicott answers that there is no real occasion for the great difficulty made about the verse: it is absurd to think of birds nesting on the altars, but quite probable that they were found in and about the temple, and he cites an old historian on nests of young sparrows taken at a Greek shrine, a story of a man slain for harming a sparrow that had sheltered in another, and a modern traveller on birds nesting in the sanctuary at Mecca. He then rules out the way Clarke prefers: the Hebrew poetic style is not favourable to simile, or the psalmist would have written, as a modern would, that as the birds delight to nest at the altars so he loves to dwell in the house. John Gill only reports that the word means any bird, that we render it sparrow and the paraphrase renders it dove.

Why the nouns stand in the plural divides four from one. John Gill, Matthew Henry, Adam Clarke and C.H. Spurgeon all explain it by the divisions of the sanctuary, the holy place and the holy of holies and the court where the people stood, Clarke including every place where acts of worship were performed. Charles Ellicott answers that the plural is used poetically and that we need not think of the courts at all, and would render the noun dwellings; John Wesley takes those who dwell there for the priests and the devout who were perpetually present; the opening word, he adds, means both loved and lovable, the Hebrew combining the two senses. He works the verb of longing the same way, from a root meaning to grow pale, so that the soul grows pale with longing, as the Latin poets used their word for pallor of passionate love, and he sets beside it a line of Shakespeare on being sicklied over with the pale cast of thought.

The title and the authorship occupy the rest. Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm at the opening of the second half of one collection, just as the psalm before closed another, and defend its stylistic character against a critic who denied it. John Calvin traces the sons named in the title to the man the earth swallowed up, whose children did not die with him and whose posterity became porters and singers; the psalm bears no author’s name, but the subject-matter fits David so well that he was in all probability its author, and the notion that the Levites composed it for his use is groundless, since one so eminently distinguished by the gift of prophecy had no need to employ them. The one difficulty he allows is the mention of the hill to which the ark was not brought until the kingdom was at peace. Augustine of Hippo had before him a title reading for the winepresses, and observes that the psalm says nothing whatever of press or basket or vat, so that other winepresses must be meant: the grape hangs on the vine and the olive on its tree enjoying a kind of free air, and neither is wine nor oil until it is pressed, and so it is with men predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son, who was himself first pressed in his Passion as the great Cluster.
5:
The clause about the ways in the heart is judged unintelligible by two of them. Adam Clarke says flatly that the received rendering is no sense, and takes the original to mean that the highways are in their hearts, that is, the roads winding to the temple, wondering whether the roads leading to the cities of refuge are in view. C.H. Spurgeon corrects it to thy ways and calls that far better. Charles Ellicott keeps the roads, deriving the word from a root meaning to cast up, so that a highway is marked by the heaps of stone piled at its side; the moral sense which the paraphrase and some moderns give it is secondary, he says, to the actual desire to join the pilgrim band, and he sets beside it the lines of Chaucer on nature pricking men in their hearts so that folk long to go on pilgrimages. John Wesley reads it as hearts set upon the city and a journey thither. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the first half instead: blessed is the man who has his strength in God, so that the strength of him to whom all things are possible is mighty in that man’s weakness.

Where the valley is, and what fills it, occupies the rest. John Gill gathers the older identifications, a valley of springs, a place of mulberry trees, the valley of the giants, and the rendering of the old versions that makes it a valley of weeping, which led some to a place named from the weeping of the people; yet he thinks no particular place is designed. Adam Clarke reports seven manuscripts that read mourning for mulberry and believes it the very place of weeping, adding that though the pilgrims pass through a barren desert they need not fear, since God opens fountains in the wilderness. Charles Ellicott weighs four identifications, a valley of trouble, the valley of the giants, one found near the mount of the law by a traveller, and one identified more recently on the caravan route from the north, and prefers the second because it is described elsewhere as sterile; the name, he adds, either plays on the sound of the word or comes from the exudations of the balsam shrub.

The second half of that verse divides them completely. Charles Ellicott holds that rain is the right rendering of the first word, and that where our version gives pools the text as it stands gives blessings, a reading now generally adopted, so that the sense is that the autumn rain covers the valley with blessings, as benign showers turn a wilderness into a garden. Adam Clarke takes the very same consonants and gets something else entirely: the instructor is covered or clothed with blessings, so that God gives his people teachers after his own heart, and while they are watering the people they are watered themselves. John Wesley and John Gill keep the pits dug for relief and the rain that fills them. The end of the following verse fares no better. Adam Clarke calls the received words a paraphrase, and a bad one, but no translation, and renders that the God of gods shall be seen in Zion; Charles Ellicott agrees that the expression is hardly Hebrew in either of its senses and that the text is suspicious, and reports an emendation to the effect that they go to the temple of the living God to see the God of gods there. John Gill instead multiplies senses for the earlier phrase, from army to army, from company to company, from victory to victory, from doctrine to doctrine, and from class to class in the school of Christ. Matthew Henry closes the passage on the prayer, taking the face of the anointed not of the psalmist himself but of the Mediator.
9:
Who the anointed is receives five answers. John Wesley takes it of the psalmist himself, who though a vile sinner is God’s anointed king. Charles Ellicott observes that shield and anointed stand in direct parallelism, so that the monarch is himself the defence spoken of. John Gill reports one Jewish commentator who understood the word of the sanctuary and another who, much better, understood it of the ruler as protector, making the petition a prayer for his preservation; but Gill prefers to apply the whole to Christ, who is called a sun and shield below. Adam Clarke reads it of the Mediator whose supplications God is asked to consider, while granting that some apply the words to the psalmist, some to the leader of the return, and some to the people, each with his reasons. C.H. Spurgeon keeps both together, calling it the nation’s prayer for its king and the believer’s prayer for the Son of David.

The comparison of the day with the thousand is taken alike by all of them. C.H. Spurgeon says the writer of course intends a thousand spent elsewhere, and that under the most favourable circumstances earthly pleasures are not comparable by so much as one in that number. Adam Clarke answers the paraphrase which made it better than so long a time in captivity, since it is better than the same anywhere at all. John Gill takes the single day of the sabbath then in being, and now of public worship, explaining the larger figure as so many common days rather than so many like it.

The next clause divides them. Charles Ellicott would render that he had rather wait upon the threshold, as one unworthy to enter the precincts, the old versions going further and making it a rejection in scorn; the notion of a doorkeeper, he grants, need not be in the Hebrew, though it suits a psalm of a family who kept the gates of the tabernacle, and he sets beside it what a Greek dramatist gives the boy who sweeps a temple step, calling that a pleasant and an honoured task. C.H. Spurgeon keeps the office and holds the lowest station about the house better than the highest among the godless, since merely to linger at the entrance and peep within is bliss. Adam Clarke turns the verse on his reader, asking who now prefers the worship of God to gay and honourable company, to feasts, to public entertainments, to the stage or the ball, and bidding conscience answer.

The sun and shield is a textual difficulty, and Adam Clarke alone treats it as one. Not a single version, he observes, renders the first word as sun; they agree generally that the Lord loveth mercy and truth, the paraphrase giving that he is as a high wall and a strong defence, and critics at large taking the term for a guard. One scholar would go further and read guardian outright, on the ground that representing God as the sun is without example in the sacred writings; but Clarke answers with the prophet who promised that the Sun of righteousness should arise with healing in his wings, and adds that no manuscript countenances the alteration. John Gill and John Wesley keep the received reading and divide the two figures between light and defence, the one enlightening and warming and cheering, the other protecting from justice and from wrath; Wesley has the first enlighten and quicken and direct, and the second save from enemies. Clarke ends where the psalm ends, on the grace that pardons and the glory that follows, and on the promise that no good thing is withheld.
